prompt:
A student estimates the volume of a standard soccer ball.
(a) The student approximates the ball as fitting snugly inside a cube of side length $20\text{ cm}$. Calculate the volume of this bounding cube in $\text{cm}^3$. [2]
(b) Explain why the actual volume of the spherical ball is smaller than the volume of the cube. [1]
(c) State a reasonable estimate for the volume of the soccer ball in $\text{cm}^3$. [1]
answer:
(a) 8000 cm^3
(b) A sphere does not fill the corners of the enclosing cube.
(c) Approximately 4000 to 5000 cm^3.

mark_scheme.criterion: (a) Shows volume formula for cube: 20 x 20 x 20.
(b) Explains that the rounded sphere leaves empty space at the corners/edges of the cube.
(c) States an estimate in the range 4000 cm^3 to 5500 cm^3 (with unit cm^3).

hints: Volume of a cube is side cubed.
Picture a ball inside a box: does the ball touch every corner?
Sphere volume is roughly half to two-thirds the cube volume.
solution:
(a) Bounding cube volume V = 20 cm x 20 cm x 20 cm = 8000 cm^3.
(b) A spherical ball only touches the cube at the center of each face. The eight corners and surrounding edges of the box are empty space, so the sphere occupies less volume than the cube.
(c) For a sphere of diameter 20 cm (radius 10 cm), V = (4/3) pi r^3 approx 4190 cm^3. A reasonable estimate is therefore about 4200 cm^3 (any value between 4000 cm^3 and 5500 cm^3 is acceptable).
teacher_walkthrough: Bounding box geometry is a foundational Cambridge spatial estimation archetype.
Ensure students understand that a sphere occupies roughly 52% of its bounding cube.
